content: Poison sumac, scientifically known as Toxicodendron vernix or Rhus vernix, is a woody shrub or small tree that can grow up to 7 meters (20 feet) in height. Every part of this plant contains a resin called urushiol, which is highly irritating to human skin and mucous membranes. When the plant is burned, inhaling the smoke can lead to diarrhea and other internal irritations. The tree has a rounded and narrow crown, with slender, pendulous branches. It often appears as a shrub. The smaller branches and young stems are pithy and contain an acrid, milky, poisonous sap that turns black upon exposure to air. The compound leaves are pinnate, measuring 25–50 cm in length, and consist of 7 to 13 leaflets. These leaflets, which are 4–10 cm long, are sometimes mistaken for individual leaves. The veins from which the leaflets grow are always red. The plant produces small white or gray berries in panicles 10–20 cm long, which distinguish it from other sumacs that bear red berries. Poison sumac also differs from other sumacs by having shorter leaves, fewer leaflets, and entire (smooth) leaflet margins. It thrives in wet soils, such as swamps and peat bogs, unlike other sumacs that prefer dry conditions. The bark of poison sumac is smooth and can range from light to dark gray, with a slightly striated appearance. The branchlets are smooth and reddish-brown, covered with small, orange-colored lenticular spots that later turn orange-brown and eventually light gray. The wood is light yellow with brown lines, light in weight, soft, coarse-grained, and brittle. The winter buds are dark purple, acute, and the terminal bud is significantly larger than the axillary buds. The leaves are alternately arranged, pinnately compound, and measure 7 to 14 inches in length. They are borne on slender, reddish petioles. Each leaf has 7 to 13 obovate or oblong leaflets, which are 3 to 4 inches long, slightly unequal or contracted at the base, with entire margins and acute or rounded apices. The terminal leaflet sometimes has a stalk up to an inch in length. When emerging from the bud, the leaves are orange-colored and downy. Once fully grown, they are smooth, dark green, and shiny on the upper surface, while pale beneath. The midrib and primary veins are prominent. In autumn, the leaves turn vibrant scarlet and orange. The flowers of poison sumac bloom in June and July. The plant is dioecious, meaning male and female flowers are borne on separate plants. The flowers are yellow-green and grow in long, narrow, axillary panicles near the ends of the branches. The bracts and bractlets are acute, downy, and fall off as the flowers open. The calyx is five-lobed, with short, acute lobes. The corolla consists of five yellow-green petals that are acute. The stamens are five in number, with long, slender filaments and large, orange-colored anthers. In fertile flowers, the stamens are short and rudimentary. The pistil has an ovoid-globose ovary that is one-celled and topped with three thick, spreading styles. The ovule is solitary. The fruit of poison sumac is a drupe, globular in shape, and white in color. It is borne in long, graceful racemes and is often tipped with the dark remnants of the styles. The fruit ripens in September and frequently remains on the tree throughout the winter. The cotyledons are flat and leaf-like. Poison sumac is found exclusively in very wet or flooded soils, typically in swamps and peat bogs, in the eastern United States and Canada. It can grow as far west as Idaho, where it is restricted to the southern part of the state. Poison sumac is classified as a noxious weed in some states due to its potential to cause urushiol-induced contact dermatitis. It is considered far more virulent than its relatives, poison ivy and poison oak. Some botanists regard poison sumac as the most toxic plant species in the United States. Exposure to the plant can result in painful and prolonged swelling and eruptions on the skin. For specific information on prevention and treatment of urushiol-induced contact dermatitis, refer to resources on this condition.
